lesson_title: Two Streets, One Country: What Development Really Measures
hook_text: South Africa has the JSE, superhighways and Sandton. So why are we called a developing country?
clip_script: Picture two streets ten minutes apart. On the first, the taps always run, the clinic is stocked and the school has a computer lab. On the second, water comes from a shared standpipe and the clinic runs dry by Thursday. Development is the work of moving the second street toward the first — and here is the catch: it is not only about money. Now watch how averages lie. Ten people share 100 rand. Everyone gets 10 each? The average is 10. One person takes 91 and nine people get one rand each? The average is STILL 10. Same average, completely different worlds. That is why geographers carry two numbers everywhere: income per person, which measures the size of the cake, and the Gini coefficient, which measures how the cake is sliced. South Africa's slice-measure is about 0,63 — one of the most unequal on the planet — and that single number explains how a middle-income country can hold both Sandton and a standpipe street in the same city. Then there is the report card with three subjects, the HDI: health, education and income averaged into one score. You cannot cram just the money subject and top the class. That is the whole game of this topic: how much a country makes, how it is shared, and what people's lives are actually like.
visual_style: A split screen of two streets morphing between scenes; animated coins stacking into two very different piles over an unchanged average line; a report card stamping three subject marks that merge into one HDI score over a map of South Africa.
mood: Eye-opening and fair-minded, ending on a challenge.
pacing: Calm two-street open, sharp beat on the 91-rand reveal, brisk close through the three questions.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and judge any country's development with four numbers.
